findings.evidence: publication_queue.py _prepare: the route is set when `conflicts and set(conflicts) <= derived_spec_paths(...)|generated`. The new handler then calls `conflicts = merge_conflicts(root, head, current_main); if conflicts: raise IntegrationRepairNeeded(...)`, so the generated-only conflicts that triggered the route are non-empty again. The test test_unavailable_derived_merge_with_a_real_conflict_needs_integration_repair uses conflicts=['src.py'], and in real _prepare that path raises at the earlier `elif conflicts:` branch. The handler should exclude derived and generated paths from the conflict set it checks.
findings.summary: The new RederivationEnvironmentFailed handler treats every non-empty merge_conflicts() result as a real conflict. But the derived-merge route is entered precisely when the conflicts are only in derived or generated paths, so a generated-only conflict (the PR #837 case) now always becomes counted integration repair instead of the uncounted environment note. This contradicts the design and spec, which say a conflict outside generated files is a real one and an environment failure spends no attempt. The regression test hides it by using conflicts=['src.py'], which can never reach the derived-merge branch.

findings.evidence: design.md of conflicting-candidate-integration-repair: 'No mergeability. ... GitHub `mergeable` is not read.' Requirement item 3: 'GitHub сообщает для него mergeable=CONFLICTING, переводится в integration red gate'.
findings.summary: Requirement item 3 is written in terms of GitHub mergeable=CONFLICTING. The T1 change deliberately never reads GitHub mergeability and relies only on the queue's own merge-tree. A candidate that GitHub reports as CONFLICTING but that merge-tree handles differently, for example a derived-merge-eligible conflict, is not routed by that signal.
